newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mercenary force assembling in Zaire, Le Monde says.
newsitem.headline: Mercenary force assembling in Zaire, Le Monde says.

text.p: A force of several hundred European and African mercenaries, some recruited by a former chief of security at the French presidency, are assembling in eastern Zaire to help stem advances by Rwanda-backed rebels, the daily Le Monde said on Tuesday.

The force numbers between 200 and 300 but is expected to grow rapidly when more men leave Europe in two weeks to join South African, French, Belgian, British, Angolan and Mozambican soldiers of fortune on the spot, the paper said.

French Cooperation Minister Jacques Godfrain said there were mercenaries from some European nations in the region but denied any official French involvement, saying Paris was victim of a smear campaign in the media.

"There are mercenaries from European countries in the region and people are pointing the finger at us when we're doing nothing," he told Reuters at a reception. He declined to say who was behind the alleged anti-French campaign.
However last October Godfrain prompted controversy when he said Washington was only interested in Africa at election time -- and when trying to curry favour with black American voters.
Washington angrily complained about his remarks.

Asked by Reuters about the report in Le Monde, the French presidency said it had no connection with, or knowledge of, a mercenary force. "If such a force exists, it is in total contradiction with French policy in the region and therefore to be condemned," a presidency spokeswoman said.
Le Monde however quoted unidentified French military sources as confirming they knew of the force's existence.
They said the force "would buy time" for the government of Zairean president Mobutu Sese Seko whose own army has performed dismally in the face of rebel advances.
France backs Mobutu politically but is officially prevented from giving him military help because of an international arms embargo on Zaire.

The newspaper quoted an unidentified senior French general as saying the mercenaries were "big-bellied ex-soldiers cashiered from the ranks...who will be unable to redress the situation in the face of a Rwandan army now equipped, trained and led on American lines."

The Le Monde report followed statements in Goma, eastern Zaire, on Monday by Laurent Kabila, head of the rebels, who said 1,000 French soldiers had arrived in Kisangani to help Zairean government forces.

French officials had denied that report, saying the only French military on Zairean soil was a handful of gendarmes guarding the French embassy in Kinshasa and the military attache in the same mission.

Le Monde said the mercenaries called their force the "White Legion" and some of its members were recruited by retired Colonel Alain Le Carro, head of the presidential guard at the Elysee palace during late president Francois Mitterrand's rule.
Le Carro, who left active service in 1994, had created a private security firm and advised the Ivory Coast and Burkina Faso governments, said Le Monde.

He worked with another former gendarme, Robert Montoya, who carried out anti-terrorism missions for the presidency and was involved in a known wiretap scandal before leaving service 10 years ago, the newspaper said.

Le Monde said the two men recruited from the same circles as had aged French "dog-of-war" Bob Denard for an unsuccessful attempt to overthrow the Comoros government in 1995 which was thwarted by the French army.
Other recruits were former members of the French Foreign Legion or Britons who had served in the Special Air Service (SAS) regiment of the British army, wrote Le Monde.
